items.title: ‘They’re Demonic’: Astronaut Who Walked on the Moon on Shocking Truth About Aliens
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "That's ... what God showed me."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former astronaut Charlie Duke is known for being the youngest man to walk on the moon. But Duke, 91, is also a strong Christian who has a fascinating perspective on aliens and UFOs, subjects that have received a plethora of attention of late.

The astronaut, who was the spacecraft communicator for the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969 and spent 265 hours in space during that time, told CBN News he once wasn’t so sure about his beliefs on the true nature of aliens and UFOs.

“For a long time [years ago] I was praying about UFOs, and asked for a sign,” Duke said. “I felt like UFOs were demonic … but I was saying that at rotary clubs and stuff like that, and people were laughing me off the stage.”

So, he asked the Lord to help him come to a definitive conclusion that would settle the matter once and for all.

“I said, ‘God, if I’m really right about this, then give me a sign tomorrow morning that a very good friend of mine at breakfast will start talking about UFOs,'” he said. “And this guy’s a businessman. He never talks about science stuff or … stuff like that. So the next morning at breakfast, we sat down, he said, ‘Charlie, come on over. I wanna start talking to you about UFOs.'”

Duke interpreted this as an answer to his prayer. The former astronaut then appealed to Scripture to make his case, looking at the Bible’s description of Satan to further conclude his position.

“The Lord says what we’re seeing is real, but the devil can appear as an angel of light, the Bible says,” he said. “And so what I believe … is the UFOs are trying to turn us away from the truth and run after these alien beings, which are really not beings at all. They’re demonic.”

Ultimately, Duke said he’s unconcerned with those who might laugh at him or mock his perspective on the matter.

“You can laugh at me if you want to, but that’s … what God showed me, and I’m sticking to it,” he said.

Duke said he never personally viewed anything on his flight to the moon that would be considered alien or UFO-like. Watch the interview above for more.

items.title: Actress Evangeline Lilly Flees Hollywood: ‘God Has a Plan’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "So intense."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Actress Evangeline Lilly has had a sweeping Hollywood career, playing beloved characters in TV shows like “Lost” and films like “The Hobbit.”

But despite a wildly popular career, Lilly decided back in 2020 to step back from Hollywood — a decision that sparked quite a bit of media interest.

“It’s been six years now,” she said, noting the media caught on to the story after she posted a retrospective in 2024. “When I was 26, I was saying … all the things I wanted in my life … and I did it … I’m there,” she said. “I’ve already retired [by 2024 when the retrospective came out]. At that point, I’ve been retired for four years … it’s been a long time of adjusting.”

Lilly said she had no idea what the “consequences” of her decision might be, though she described moments of fear as she “let go of so much … power, influence, and potential money.” There was also the affirmation piece of the puzzle.

“When you’re successful at something, it feels really good when the world says, ‘We love you! You’re amazing!’ Like, this is a wonderful feeling,” Lilly said. “How do you walk away from that? And I’ve had moments of … gripping fear of like, ‘What am I doing?’ But, ultimately, the decision was one that was made in great conviction.

Before becoming an actress, Lilly studied political science and international relations and wanted to become a missionary, humanitarian, or diplomat.

“I wanted to make the world a better place,” she said. “And there are many people who will claim that actors are making the world a better place, that they’ve had an impact on their lives. But…I’ve always wanted a much more hands-on impact. I’ve done 22 years of hands-on humanitarian work in Rwanda.”

But Lilly said she wants to do more and wants to help people heal and find wholeness.

“I love telling stories, but I’d like to tell stories of my own instead of being in front of the camera,” she said. “I’d much prefer a quieter position. I’ve always hated being famous. I never made any secrets about that. I’ve always said being famous is the cost of the wealth that you can get as an actor. Like that’s what you pay for — the wealth.”

Now, she feels liberated and said she has stepped into a “total trust and surrender that God has a plan for my life.”

Despite mostly stepping out of Hollywood, Lilly is now lending her voice to a different type of project: “Legend of Destruction,” a film that tells the “story of the Jewish revolt against Rome, which ended with the destruction of the Temple in the year 70.”

“The film was originally made in Hebrew, and so I actually was able to see the fully completed piece before I came on board for the English version,” she told CBN News. “I didn’t understand what I was looking at. I didn’t understand what I was being invited into, but I watched the film, and within the first…three to four seconds of the film, I felt like I was just completely immersed in a way that most films don’t do for me anymore.”

What makes “Legend of Destruction” unique is that it’s made of still paintings, with Lilly, who portrays Queen Bernice, and other actors using their voices to dramatically retell the story.

“This story was so intense and beautifully told, and then also incredibly timely because it’s talking about a society divided unto itself,” Lilly said. “So a society that’s really broken and in civil strife and how that leads ultimately to mutual destruction amongst all of its people.”

Given that the film deals with the destruction of the Second Temple, many people will be interested in this unique film.

“At that time, Jerusalem was under threat from the Roman Empire. The Romans were coming to destroy the temple and to take over the city,” Lilly said. “The outcome of that could have potentially been different had the Israeli people been unified, but they were so disenchanted, they were so disenfranchised from one another, they were so divided that they were actually killing each other before the Romans ever even got a chance to arrive. It’s an incredible story. That’s what drew me in.”

The “Lost” star said the events in “Legend of Destruction” take place about 33 years after Christ’s death, meaning they are very much part of the world Jesus was born into.

items.title: Jess Connolly: The People Preaching Are Scared, Too
items.author: Jess Connolly
items.summary: I was standing on stage a few months ago, my hands gently trembling as I prepared to teach a room full of high-capacity leaders. I’d been invited to speak to C-suite executives and some of the most influential pastors in the country about fear, and I wanted to do it well. My message grew out…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

I was standing on stage a few months ago, my hands gently trembling as I prepared to teach a room full of high-capacity leaders. I’d been invited to speak to C-suite executives and some of the most influential pastors in the country about fear, and I wanted to do it well.

My message grew out of years of coaching and research, and the work that led me to write You Can’t Be Brave Until You’re Scared. But its effectiveness relied on one variable: the people sitting in front of me would have to admit they were scared. These were people who didn’t often publicly acknowledge weakness.

I could tell early on that I didn’t have them. I heard fabric rustling and forks clinking against plates. I needed to help them see why processing fear mattered more than continuing to stuff it down. So I pulled out my metaphorical hammer and placed it on the table.

“How many of you have ever gone to the ER, certain you were having a heart attack, only to discover it was panic?”

Some giggled, unsure whether I was serious. I was incredibly serious. I’d heard versions of this story from so many high-capacity leaders.

“I’m serious,” I repeated. “How many of you? Maybe you didn’t make it all the way to the ER, but you seriously considered it?”

I wasn’t shaming them, and I think they knew it. I was asking because I cared.

The air went still. Nearly every hand in the room went up.

I’ve been leading in the local church in some capacity for two decades. When I say there’s a problem with how we’re handling fear, the call is coming from inside the house. I’ve been part of the problem, and I want to be part of the solution.

We’ve slapped platitudes and acronyms onto the hearts of terrified people while wrestling with anxiety ourselves. We’ve used fear to make poignant points in sermons, then shamed listeners for not having more trust. We’ve preached supernatural faith without explaining what it might look like to practice it. We’ve said God made our bodies good, but failed to compassionately shepherd people when those good bodies experience anxiety.

We need a better conversation about fear.

A few years ago, I began researching fear theologically, biblically, physiologically, and practically. I didn’t want to keep offering bumper-sticker phrases when we could ask better questions and find better answers. Four discoveries have changed the way I think about courage.

First, feeling fear is not a sin.

Fear is a natural, often involuntary response to a perceived threat. Before we’ve evaluated whether something is dangerous, our nervous systems may already be responding. Our hearts race, our hands tremble, and our bodies prepare to protect us.

Yet we’ve often treated these sensations as evidence of a spiritual problem, assuming that if we trusted God more, our bodies wouldn’t respond this way. But a racing heart is not a confession of unbelief. An anxious nervous system is not proof of failed faith.

What we believe about our fears and choose to do with them matters deeply. Experiencing fear, however, is not the same as choosing to be governed by it.

Second, the Bible’s commands about fear are invitations to trust, not weapons for shame.

Scripture repeatedly tells us not to fear and not to be anxious. We should take those words seriously, while paying attention to the people receiving them.

God tells Joshua not to fear as he prepares to lead people into an uncertain future. Angels tell terrified people not to fear. Jesus tells His disciples not to let their hearts be troubled, even as He prepares them for suffering. These words aren’t spoken because the circumstances are imaginary. They’re reminders of who God is in the middle of them.

And then there’s Jesus in Gethsemane.

The Gospels describe Him as deeply distressed and sorrowful as He approaches the cross. He doesn’t pretend the suffering ahead is insignificant. He names His anguish, brings it before His Father, and asks His friends to stay near Him in prayer. His distress is real, and so is His obedience.

We shouldn’t collapse biblical anguish into a modern clinical diagnosis. But Jesus shows us that profound distress and perfect faithfulness are not opposites.

Perhaps we’ve been so eager to teach people not to be afraid that we’ve forgotten to teach them what to do when they are.

Third, our obsession with fearlessness is hurting the people we lead and love.

We admire the fearless pastor, the confident executive, the Christian who always seems certain of the next step. But fearlessness isn’t the same as courage. And people who can’t acknowledge their fear may become especially vulnerable to being directed by it.

Unacknowledged fear can look like control, defensiveness, people-pleasing, or an inability to have difficult conversations. Sometimes the person who appears most confident is working hardest to avoid something they’re terrified might happen.

This isn’t just about pastors. We all influence someone, whether we’re raising children, serving a neighbor, leading a team, or showing up for a friend. Our fear doesn’t stay neatly contained inside us. It can shape the atmosphere around us.

We don’t need more fearless Christians. We need more Christians who know what to do when they’re afraid.

Fourth, paying attention to fear may be one of the most practical ways to practice courage.

Many of us have been taught to dismiss fear quickly. We quote a verse, remind ourselves that God is in control, and try to move on. Scripture is essential to our faith, but sometimes we’ve used true words to avoid honest conversations.

What if, instead of immediately silencing fear, we got curious about it?

What am I actually afraid will happen? What feels threatened? What am I believing about God, myself, or other people? And if the thing I’m afraid of happens, what would faithfulness look like then?

Naming fear doesn’t mean agreeing with everything it tells us. It means bringing it into the light, where we can examine it and respond thoughtfully.

Sometimes courage looks like taking the next step while our hands are trembling. Sometimes it looks like asking for help, seeking counseling or medical care, or admitting that the way we’ve been living is no longer sustainable.

Kingdom courage isn’t the absence of fear. It’s the willingness to move toward faithfulness in its presence, trusting God as we go.

Back on stage, as those leaders slowly lowered their hands, I knew I had their attention. I led them through a practical exercise: name the fear, consider the worst-case scenario, and decide what courage might look like moving forward.

It wasn’t all the work, but it was a start.

The change in the room was palpable. The mood felt lighter, the resistance was gone, and so was the pretense. I reminded them that fear didn’t disqualify them from leadership, but refusing to acknowledge it could deeply affect the people they were called to serve.

The same is true for you and me.

We are scared. There’s no getting around it. Pretending otherwise doesn’t just harm us. It shapes our churches, families, teams, and communities in ways we may not recognize.

I keep thinking about that room and all those raised hands. I wonder how many people there had spent years believing they were the only ones. I wonder how many people sitting in our churches believe the same thing.

Maybe the bravest thing we could do for the people around us is to stop pretending we’re not scared.

May the culture of modern-day followers of Jesus become more informed, more honest, more compassionate, and more courageous.

In Jesus’ name.

Jess Connolly is the author of You Can’t Be Brave Until You’re Scared (Baker Books), out now, as well as Tired of Being Tired and What Comes Next. She and her husband, Nick, planted Bright City Church in Charleston, South Carolina. She leads Go + Tell Gals and hosts The Jess Connolly Podcast. Find her at JessConnolly.com or on Instagram @JessAConnolly.

items.title: The Fall Ball Blues: Vulgarity at the Plate
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

There have been recent incidents that have gone viral over inappropriate walk-up music in youth baseball.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

When first yellows creep across wooded scenes,
Backdrop to flying white spheres with red seams.
When leaves dance to whooshes of full count swings,
And choruses cheer as metal bat sings.
Then you will know the joy this season brings.
Fall baseball!

. . . Or so I believed.

As my eight-year-old was warming up for a fall ball game recently, the air was filled not with the idyllic sounds of the season punctuated by children laughing and satisfying pops of gloves sticking baseballs. Rather, everyone’s ears were filled with the obnoxiously loud music being played by the opposing team. In my experience, wannabe DJs have become more common in little league. Usually, I try to ignore the self-appointed noise polluters. But this time was different. All of a sudden the following lyrics rang out: 

And I’m on this foolish track, so I spit my foolish flow
My hands go up and down, like strippers’ booties go

I made a beeline for the parents near the giant speaker. “Excuse me!” I yelled, not out of anger so much as to be heard over the cacophonous track. “It doesn’t seem appropriate to play music talking about strippers around eight- and nine-year-olds! I would respectfully request something more age appropriate!” 

The parents and coach gawked at me. I must have seemed to them as that guy—the old fuddy-duddy. But their appearance to the world was perhaps even more shocking, since the cross of our Lord was prominently emblazoned on the sleeves of their jerseys. One of them muttered something that sounded like “Okay,” as I turned to return to help coach my team. That seemed to be that. But, not a week later, I was sitting as a spectator for my eleven-year-old son’s game. My son was on the mound getting ready to face the first batter of the inning when the opposing team’s speaker bellowed, “Now, baby, get butt-booty naked, take off all your clothes.” 

Again? This was not what little league fall baseball was supposed to sound like. Indeed, I had never even heard such filth in a major-league ballpark. “Excuse me,” I asked the woman with the speaker, “Why do you think it is appropriate to play music about women taking off all their clothes for eleven-year-olds?” Again, the silent gawk—but this time, an older woman behind her retorted, “How dare you walk up to a woman and question her?” That took me aback. So apparently this fake feminist’s argument was that it was good and right to play modern musical masterpieces in which women are instrumentalized as objects of male sexual conquest—and it was sexist for a man to question it. I quickly realized, though, that these women likely felt pangs of shame, but instead of apologize or even attempt to defend the indefensible, they attacked me personally. I removed myself and simply reported the incident to the commissioner (who, thankfully, took measures to put a stop to it).

While my story is just one anecdote, it is notable that there have been recent incidents that have gone viral over inappropriate walk-up music in youth baseball. Last spring, a conscientious coach asked for inappropriate walk-up music to stop, and when the umpire did nothing, he chose to forfeit the game instead. In another piece of evidence spotlighting the decline of moral standards among little league parents, a New York Times report on the restaurant chain Hooters noted examples of coaches and parents taking youth baseball teams there for postgame celebrations. 

While it arguably does not have the pride of place it once did in American culture, it cannot be denied that baseball is historically America’s pastime. It is a game, as Ken Burns noted, that follows the seasons: “beginning each year with the fond expectancy of springtime, and ending with the hard facts of autumn.” As Burns’s singular documentary points out, as a leisurely pastoral game played with lightning speed in American cities, it is a metaphor for many tensions or contradictions held together by the American idea. As a uniquely American game that Americans have played for over two hundred years, it binds the generations. And as a game in which the best hitters fail two-thirds of the time, and the very best teams lose a third of their games, it is a game in which the young learn the meaning of failure and success, sorrow and hope. Indeed, some theologians have argued that baseball is something of a metaphor for the journey of the Christian soul. The soul “goes out” (exitus) from the Creator, and its destiny is to return (reditus) home. Yet, postlapsarian man’s journey is riddled with more failures than successes. Still, the outpouring of grace and forgiveness fits the wayfarer with a clean slate to begin anew, symbolized by each time one steps up to the plate. And the idea of the “sacrifice” (a sac-fly or sac-bunt), is a metaphor for gift-love, of laying one’s life down for one’s friends.

Much more could be said along these lines, but suffice it to say that baseball is more than just another game. It has a heritage that parents and coaches are stewards of and which they pass down to their children and players. Christian parents in particular coach and support this game not merely as a fun break from the duties of school and work, but as an aspect of their God-given duty to raise their sons to become men of virtue. Is it not obvious, therefore, that Christian parents and coaches bear a grave responsibility in how they manage their little leagues? Not only do they owe something to their ancestors who devised and passed down such a brilliant game, but they owe it to their players—and the opposing team’s players—to facilitate all the virtues baseball can teach them. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Lewd walk-up music of the sort discussed above undermines all of this. Instead of the basic equal human dignity that is the legacy of the stories of greats like Jackie Robinson, it treats women like second-class citizens, like mere objects of sexual gratification. Instead of the calming, leisurely, cerebral, and almost liturgical rhythms of pitch, ball, strike, out, and inning—which appeal to and cultivate the soul’s higher faculties—its agitated beats and vulgar lyrics basely appeal to sexual desire, conquest, and gratification. Whereas the game of baseball teaches young men that they ought to use their strength for the good of others (the team), such noisy excrement instructs them to pursue their selfish desires. Instead of honoring the dignity of the team in which sex is properly placed (the institution of marriage), it cheapens and commercializes this most sacred of God’s gifts to man. 

A few days ago, I sat spectating with a jacket on, the chilled air portending autumn’s end as orange leaves blew around my feet. The field had been pulsating with the beats of strikes to the catcher’s mitt. My eleven-year-old had just finished pitching two shutout innings before I arrived. It was that same team he played a few weeks ago. But it seemed quiet as I sat down. Were those angry eyes I could feel staring across the diamond because not one of their kids could manage a hit? Or was it because the fuddy-duddy dad who had complained about their loutish behavior had just arrived? I didn’t much care either way. Then they fired up their new in-between inning music. “Baby shark, doo-doo doo-doo doo-doo . . . ” 

I leaned back in my rocker chair and chuckled. Well, at least it’s not strippers. Then, as the hook repeated, I sighed. Perhaps this is what the late fall ball blues is supposed to sound like. I suppose I’m ready for the hard facts of autumn to become the cold truth of winter.

items.title: Wednesday, October 21, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, the Lord urges his disciples and us to be prudent servants, following his ways in anticipation of his coming again.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 3:2-12

For surely you have already heard of the commission of God’s grace that was given me for you, and how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I wrote above in a few words, a reading of which will enable you to perceive my understanding of the mystery of Christ. In former generations this mystery was not made known to humankind, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit: that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

Of this gospel I have become a servant according to the gift of God’s grace that was given me by the working of his power. Although I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ, and to make everyone see what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God who created all things; so that through the church the wisdom of God in its rich variety might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. This was in accordance with the eternal purpose that he has carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have access to God in boldness and confidence through faith in him.

Psalm
Isaiah 12:2-3, 4bcd, 5-6

Surely God is my salvation;
    I will trust, and will not be afraid,
for the Lord God is my strength and my might;
    he has become my salvation.
With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.
And you will say in that day:
Give thanks to the Lord,
    call on his name;
make known his deeds among the nations;
    proclaim that his name is exalted.
Sing praises to the Lord, for he has done gloriously;
    let this be known in all the earth.
Shout aloud and sing for joy, O royal Zion,
    for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.

Gospel Reading
Luke 12:39-48

“But know this: if the owner of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an unexpected hour.”

Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for everyone?” And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and prudent manager whom his master will put in charge of his slaves, to give them their allowance of food at the proper time? Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives. Truly I tell you, he will put that one in charge of all his possessions. But if that slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and if he begins to beat the other slaves, men and women, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know, and will cut him in pieces, and put him with the unfaithful. That slave who knew what his master wanted, but did not prepare himself or do what was wanted, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know and did what deserved a beating will receive a light beating. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be demanded.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, the Lord urges his disciples and us to be prudent servants, following his ways in anticipation of his coming again. Theologians often call prudence the queen of the virtues because it is the capacity to reign sovereignly over one’s life, both ordering one’s inner powers and directing one’s affairs wisely in the outside world.

Prudence is that sure touch, that moral instinct that renders one capable of making the right decision under pressure and in the face of complex circumstances. Prudence is a sort of accumulated theoretical and practical wisdom, a know-how that is for the most part instinctual, in the bones.

When placed in the Christian context, therefore, prudence is a feel for how Jesus would react, how he would think, how he would move in a particular situation. It is tantamount to having one’s soul gathered around Christ as its center, so that all one’s actions are informed by Jesus and his way of being in the world. Christian prudence comes from apprenticing to Christ—that is to say, moving in with him, watching at close quarters how he lives and moves and gestures.
